dataset_example.prompt: [{'role': 'user', 'content': 'I earn $4,500/month after tax. My rent is $1,400, car payment $350, groceries $400, utilities $150, subscriptions $80, and I have $2,000 in credit card debt at 22% APR. How should I budget the rest and tackle my debt?'}]
dataset_example.answer: Allocate remaining $1,120: pay minimum on credit card ($50), put $500 extra toward credit card debt (avalanche method, highest APR first), build a $1,000 emergency fund with $400/month over 2.5 months, then redirect that to debt. Cut subscriptions to essentials. Target: debt-free in ~4 months, then build 3-month emergency fund ($5,100).

items.answer: Index funds are recommended for most investors. Historical data shows 90%+ of actively managed funds underperform the S&P 500 over 15+ years. Your friend's Tesla gain is survivorship bias — many individual stock pickers lose money. A total market index fund (like VTI) gives instant diversification across 3,500+ stocks at 0.03% expense ratio. If you want some individual stocks, limit to 5-10% of your portfolio as 'play money' you can afford to lose.

prompt.content: Should I invest in individual stocks or index funds? My friend made 200% on Tesla last year.

items.answer: Priority order: (1) Contribute 6% to 401k to get full employer match (free money, ~$5,100/year), (2) Max out Roth IRA ($7,000/year for 2024), (3) Build 6-month emergency fund ($21K at $3,500/month expenses), (4) Increase 401k toward $23,500 limit, (5) Open taxable brokerage for additional investing. For allocation: 80/20 stocks/bonds at age 28, use low-cost index funds (total market + international).
